speaker: tech
text: Hi, I'm Jordan, I'll be helping Doctor Okafor today. So we have Pickles and Olive. Who's here for what?

speaker: client
text: Olive is here for her yearly checkup and vaccines. Pickles is the older one, and he's been limping on his back leg.

speaker: tech
text: Okay. Let me get weights on both. Olive first. Olive is three point nine kilos. And Pickles is six point three kilos.

speaker: tech
text: How long has Pickles been limping?

speaker: client
text: About two weeks. It's his right back leg. It's worse in the morning, and he doesn't jump onto the bed anymore.

speaker: tech
text: Got it. Any vomiting, diarrhea, or changes in appetite for either of them?

speaker: client
text: No, both are eating fine. Pickles might be eating a bit less, but he's also less active.

speaker: tech
text: Okay. Doctor Okafor will be right in.

speaker: dvm
text: Hello! Nice to meet you. Jordan filled me in. Let's start with Olive, since she's the easy one, and then spend some time on Pickles.

speaker: client
text: Sounds good.

speaker: dvm
text: How old is Olive now?

speaker: client
text: She's four. She's spayed, indoor only.

speaker: dvm
text: Any concerns with her at all? Litter box, coughing, sneezing, scratching?

speaker: client
text: Nothing. She's perfect. Maybe a little chubby.

speaker: dvm
text: Let's see. Her temperature is thirty-eight point four, heart rate is one hundred eighty. Her ears are clean, eyes clear. Her teeth look good, no tartar to speak of.

speaker: dvm
text: Heart sounds normal, lungs clear. Her belly is soft. I'd say her body condition is five out of nine, so she's actually right where she should be.

speaker: client
text: Oh good. I'll tell my partner she's not chubby.

speaker: dvm
text: She's fluffy, not chubby. For vaccines, she's due for her F V R C P booster today, which covers the upper respiratory viruses and panleukopenia. Her rabies is good until next spring.

speaker: client
text: Okay, let's do the F V R C P.

speaker: dvm
text: Jordan, could you draw that up for Olive?

speaker: tech
text: Sure. F V R C P for Olive, right front leg, under the skin?

speaker: dvm
text: Yes, please, right front leg.

speaker: tech
text: Done. She didn't even notice.

speaker: dvm
text: Good girl. Now, Pickles. How old is he?

speaker: client
text: He's fourteen. Neutered. Also indoors.

speaker: dvm
text: Has he ever had a problem with that leg before? Any falls you know of?

speaker: client
text: Not that I know of. He jumped down from the top of the fridge a while ago, but that was months back.

speaker: dvm
text: Does the limp improve once he's been moving for a while?

speaker: client
text: Yes, actually. After he's walked around for ten minutes he seems a lot better. In the morning he's really stiff.

speaker: dvm
text: That pattern sounds like arthritis. Is he still using his litter box normally? Sometimes cats with sore joints start going outside the box because the sides are too high.

speaker: client
text: Now that you mention it, he peed next to the box twice last week.

speaker: dvm
text: That fits. Is he drinking more water than usual, or peeing larger amounts?

speaker: client
text: Maybe a little more water. I've been filling his bowl more often.

speaker: dvm
text: Okay, I'll keep that in mind. Let me look at him. His temperature is thirty-eight point two. Heart rate is one hundred sixty, respiratory rate is twenty-eight.

speaker: dvm
text: I hear a soft heart murmur, grade two out of six, on the left side. I don't think we've recorded that before. His lungs sound clear.

speaker: client
text: A murmur? Is that serious?

speaker: dvm
text: Not necessarily. In older cats it can be from thickened heart muscle or high blood pressure, or it can be harmless. We'll check his blood pressure today, and I'll talk about further tests in a moment.

speaker: dvm
text: His body condition is four out of nine, and he's lost muscle over his back and back legs. Six point three kilos, and in January he was six point eight.

speaker: dvm
text: Now the legs. He's sore when I flex and extend his right knee, and I can feel some thickening around the joint. I don't feel a cruciate ligament tear, there's no drawer movement. His left knee is a little stiff too. His hips move freely, and he has normal feeling in his feet.

speaker: dvm
text: Both knees are uncomfortable, the right more than the left. I'd give him a pain score of two out of four on the right knee.

speaker: tech
text: Doctor, his blood pressure reading came back at one hundred seventy-five.

speaker: dvm
text: Thank you, Jordan. That's elevated. Over one hundred sixty in a cat puts him at risk of damage to the eyes, kidneys, and heart. Combined with drinking more and the weight loss, I want to check his kidneys and thyroid.

speaker: client
text: Okay. What tests does he need?

speaker: dvm
text: Today I'd recommend a chemistry panel with S D M A, a complete blood count, a thyroid level, and a urinalysis with a urine protein ratio. I'd also like x-rays of both knees to confirm arthritis and rule out anything else in the bone.

speaker: dvm
text: Because of the murmur and the blood pressure, I'd also recommend an echocardiogram, an ultrasound of the heart. That would be with the cardiologist who visits on Tuesdays.

speaker: client
text: Let's do the bloodwork, the urine, and the x-rays today. Can I think about the heart ultrasound?

speaker: dvm
text: Absolutely. I'll write that down as recommended, and you'll let us know. If he has trouble breathing, or suddenly can't use his back legs, that's an emergency.

speaker: client
text: Okay. Wait, can't use his back legs, why would that happen?

speaker: dvm
text: Rarely, cats with heart disease form a blood clot that blocks blood flow to the back legs. It's sudden and very painful. I'm not saying that's what's happening, his limp is gradual and fits arthritis, but I want you to know the warning signs.

speaker: client
text: Okay, that's good to know.

speaker: dvm
text: For his pain, I don't want to give him an anti-inflammatory until we know his kidney values. Today I'd like to start him on a monthly injection called frunevetmab, which is an antibody that targets arthritis pain. It's safe for the kidneys.

speaker: client
text: Yes, let's do that. He's clearly uncomfortable.

speaker: dvm
text: Jordan, could you get the frunevetmab? He's six point three kilos, so he gets the dose for cats between two and a half and seven kilos, one full vial, under the skin.

speaker: tech
text: On it. Under the skin, left side.

speaker: dvm
text: We'll repeat that every four weeks. Most cats show improvement after the first or second injection.

speaker: dvm
text: At home, put a litter box with a low side near where he sleeps. Add a ramp or a step stool near the bed and his favorite window, and give him soft bedding.

speaker: client
text: I can do that. What about the blood pressure? Do we treat that today?

speaker: dvm
text: I'd like to confirm it with the bloodwork first. If his kidney or thyroid values are abnormal, that changes the plan. I'll call you with the results tomorrow, and we'll likely start a blood pressure medication called amlodipine.

speaker: client
text: Okay.

speaker: dvm
text: Jordan will take Pickles back for his x-rays and the blood and urine samples. It takes about forty minutes, and you can wait here or come back.

speaker: client
text: I'll wait. Olive can keep me company.

speaker: dvm
text: Perfect. For Olive, keep doing what you're doing. We'll see her next year. For Pickles, his next frunevetmab injection is in four weeks, and I'd like to recheck his blood pressure in two weeks if we start the amlodipine.

speaker: client
text: Got it. Thank you, Doctor Okafor.

speaker: tech
text: I'll bring Pickles back out once the x-rays are done.
